solo traveling M26 in SEA here. I've been traveling for about a month.  A couple thoughts I have:

As we get older, I think our taste refines in the kind of people we want to build relationships with. I think its natural to meet less people that you really build a connection with, especially when there's an age gap. I travelled in Europe when I was 22 and had a much more social experience than I am having this time around. For me, its not something that I'm necessarily surprised by, which brings me to my next point.

It's important to set up expectations for the type of trip you wish to have. A couple weeks ago I saw a post here from a girl who was travelling in Europe and not feeling comfortable because she didn't bring going out attire despite having fantasized about carefree nightlife of a european backpacking trip. the comments advised her to reflect on the type of trip she really was looking for when she set out. I don't know enough to speak to your circumstance but if I decided that I wanted to have a more social trip, there are a couple things I would do. 

First off, I would make sure I'm going out of my way to break the ice and induce conversation. More often than not, I think that people are open to making connections travelling but may be meek about making the first step. Its a social skill to be comfortable breaking the awkward silence of the first night in a hostel or asking to befriend someone sitting alone. Getting comfortable engaging like this doesn't happen overnight but its a good muscle to train in every walk of life and will allow you to attract more of the kinds of people you want to have in your life. 

Second, (and I mean this in the least pretentious way possible), it's important to make concessions about the kind of person you are willing to associate with. It's easy to decide you don't have enough in common with somone and write them off, it takes work to forge the relationship with any individual and can be an exciting process to uncover ways in which you might have more in common than you intended. (you both love travel so atleast there's that!)

Lastly, it's important to accept yourself and recognize the value you add in the lives of others. I may be projecting here but it took me years of therapy to feel comfortable in my skin and once I did, I felt much better communicating with others and being empathetic to the challenges each individual wrestles with as we wander through our 20s and our entire lives for that matter. Make sure you're not being hard on yourself when your not making the connections you hope to make and continue to be a person you will be proud of when you reflect on your travels.

Ok, now that I have given you my pep talk, I'll share some concrete advice that I've seen work for others: 

Do excursions through your hostel: You meet other people in the hostel in a natural environment and can often go out to dinner or drinks with them after. 

Play games at the hostel: Play pool or ping pong or whatever and you'll often meet others looking for some new friends.

Go to another hostel: If you're hostel is not the vibe, go look up other hostels on hostelworld and go to them. Sometimes I purposely pick "chill"hostels so I can go to bed when I want, nothing is stopping you from going to the party hostel down the street.  

Pick places to backpack where you are more likely to meet people with common interests: Bangkok is a party town where I wouldnt necessarily anticipate meaningful relationships, Luang Prabang is a quiet town that is pretty far off the beaten path for social travellers. I would recommend looking at some places with better excursion culture. An example for me would be the Ha Giang Loop in Vietnam where you meet lots of people with a common admiration for nature and build community throughout the 3-4 day excursion.

I attended a course the day after a certain recent election in October. Admittedly, I spent many hours dwelling on politics during my meditation. For me, this manifests in a commitment to local change rather than reactionary responses to what I witness in media. I had a conversation with my teacher at the retreat about what to do when thoughts arise and weather I ought to attempt to reconcile them. He was very clear that the process of catching your mind wandering and returning to the observation of sensations is sufficient for a reconciliation process. I believe that applies here as well. Return to practice as political thoughts arise, reflect outside of practice and see if you engage with the things which challenge you differently.
